articles.title: French High School Students Lead Mass Protests over School Funding, Inequality; Thousands Arrested
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : Nearly 2,000 French high schools are blockaded or closed today as massive student-led protests spread over France over school funding and inequality. The demonstration began in September at a single school outside Paris, where students protested teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school buildings. But the scope of the protests has widened amidst a violent crackdown by French police. French authorities have arrested more than 5,000 people since the movement began, about 85% of them high schoolers. These are the voices of two students protesting in Paris earlier today. HUGO VETZEL : [translated] For us, it’s, first of all, in support of the high school students who started blockades a few days ago. I think we all have a role to play in this movement, and the more we are, the more we will be heard. And I think this is not a fight of a few handful of people, but a more global fight for the youth. … We feel despised, because when the answer is violence, that means, in a way, democracy is no longer working. But we feel especially that there is such a gap between the elites and us, and we feel we are creating unease, because we are disrupting so much that they are using force to shut us up. MONA FALLACARA : [translated] I am quite happy because, for once, we see a real movement of the youth everywhere, and we hear about it. But then, what I deplore is that the media is showing more of the violence done by the students before their demands, which are vital. And yes, there is a bit of violence, but it’s not everywhere. … France’s budget will come to a vote soon, so we hope there will be a higher budget for education. And for the presidential election next year, as well, we hope for a bit of change after 10 years of President Macron heading the country. AMY GOODMAN : France’s official independent national human rights body has expressed deep concern over what it called the state’s disproportionate use of force in response to the protests. On Monday, Democracy Now! reached a French student who described the violent police crackdown. For her safety, she asked not to be identified. PROTESTER : During the protests, people, students receive tear gas, receive — like, get hit, get attacked, get charged by policemen, by the CRS , which is a police institution. And yes, basically it has been really violent. Many people have been wounded. Many people have been arrested. Someone lost an eye. Someone lost a hand. And this is happening to literal teens, literal children. We even — most of us aren’t even adults yet. And this is terrible, because literal adult people, adult policemen, adult policewomen, with weapons and tear gas and shields and helmets, are attacking literal students with some — some cardboard with messages on it. Like, we’re pacifists, and our movement is nonviolent, and yet we receive so much violence, violence from the government. AMY GOODMAN : That was a French high school student afraid to be named or shown. We go now to France. We begin with Claire Vigneau, the general secretary of the French student union, the FSE . She’s at a protest in Rennes, in northwestern France. Thanks so much for joining us, Claire. If you can start off by talking about how these protests began? When people hear “suburbs,” they think more middle-class, but in France, it’s basically the opposite, where more poverty is concentrated. Talk about the schools, the high school students and how this has grown. CLAIRE VIGNEAU : Yeah, so, it started like a few days ago, and maybe 10 days ago, something like that. And now it’s getting bigger and bigger every day. Yes, it started in Saint-Denis, which is a suburbs near Paris, but very poor suburbs. And it started because class conditions, like studying conditions, are really getting worse and worse. And, like, there is water in their class. They have rats in their class. The roof is falling out. And yeah, so it’s getting harder and harder to study for these high school students. And so they started to block their high schools. And now it’s widened out to most of the high schools in France. Actually, today, the state decided to close 500 high schools, because they didn’t want them to be blocked. But even with that precaution, 500 more high schools are blocked. And for now, we are — for now we are — we have also like 90% of the universities, the campuses that are blocked. And we are going to keep on going yet, keep on going to block. Today, we were on a protest in Rennes, yes. We are trying to escape from the policemen that are chasing us with tear gas and with cannon, water cannon. And so, yes, it was a very big protest in Rennes. There was actually like 16,000 people in Rennes, which is not a big city. And one thing to note is that the minister of the interior told today the head of the biggest trade union in France that Rennes was going to be an example of repression, of violence, and to show all the rest of the movement that we can’t do what we are doing now, which is protest for our living conditions. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Claire, could you talk more about what the demands of the students are, and especially their concerns about so many of these schools having no air conditioning in warm weather, that the heat gets up to 35 degrees Celsius, or 95 degrees Fahrenheit, especially given that France has had so many people die during heat waves this past year? CLAIRE VIGNEAU : Yeah, yeah, because we have seen a lot of classes, even in classes for like really young child, starting from 6 years old, being in classrooms where there were like 35 students with temperatures attaining 35 degrees and even more — some of them attained 40 degrees. And we are concerned, because you can’t learn, really, in a really good way when you are under this weather. And we are fighting, of course, for the weather conditions, like the stunning conditions, but not only. And obviously, we are struggling for more budgets in school and less budgets in the Army, because in France the financement for the Army doubled in 10 years, and when they — at the same time, the budgets for education is getting lower and lower every day. And so, that’s like — the air conditioning is, of course, one of the goals, but not only. And before even having air conditioning, we would like to have safe classrooms with no bad products for our health in the buildings. And we would like, if it rains outside, we don’t want rain in our classrooms, etc., etc. AMY GOODMAN : We’re going to go right now to southern France, where we’re joined by Cole Stangler, a journalist in France covering politics and labor. The significance of this protest call? I mean, we see Claire in the streets of Rennes. There are protests in Lille, a nationwide day of protests, the college unions and other labor unions joining in these protests right now, thousands of people arrested, about 5,000, over 87% of them kids in high school. COLE STANGLER : Yeah, that’s right. And I think maybe just to complement some of what we’ve been — already been hearing, you know, those issues have been absolutely at the forefront of what I’ve been hearing on the ground here. I was just at a protest in Aix-en-Provence, just in the south of France, just north of Marseille, where students were telling me their own stories of the dilapidated conditions of some of their buildings, which, to be fair, aren’t nearly as bad as when we talk about the suburbs of Paris, where you have, you know, rats in the hallways, but still, people talking about dilapidated buildings, having to install nets around their — around the buildings to make sure there’s not falling debris. That’s an issue I heard about. And, you know, another issue people talk a lot about here is the staff shortages, the lack of teachers. This has been an issue that’s been bubbling up for years, in fact. And we heard it mentioned, France’s — the amount of spending that France has done on education has stagnated, if not declined. You know, if you go back to the late '90s, 1997, France was spending over 7% of its GDP on education. That's declined about nearly a percentage point. So, the government is spending less, and the salaries are quite low, as well. That might be shocking to some viewers in the United States. You know, a starting salary for a public school teacher in France is around 2,000 euros. Even mid-career professionals are making less than the OECD average, less than the European Union average. And so, when you have low salaries, you know, and you have dilapidated buildings, it’s easy to maybe understand why you have these staff shortages. And so, this is an interesting issue where the critiques that high school students are making are actually very similar to what teachers’ unions have been saying for quite some time. So, there’s that issue of the shortages. And I think another key issue that’s emerged — and again, students were talking about it, both the high school students I talked to earlier today and the university students who joined the protests — was the issue of what in France they call Parcoursup, which is the new platform that was introduced a few years ago, which is basically an application platform for high school students to get into universities, that is not very transparent. There’s a lot of critiques about how this sort of seemingly mysterious system will offer university spots to students. So, students aren’t getting to go to the universities they want to go to that are close to them. They might have to move halfway across the country. That means more money that they’re spending on rent; they can’t live with their parents. And so, that critique of the university application process is something that unites, again, both high school students and university students. And that’s what’s been interesting when you’re talking to people on the streets here, is to see to what extent the high school student issues actually resonate beyond just high schools. Right? It’s university students. It’s also trade unions. Today, at the protest I was at, you had a lot of trade union support from, you know, the main labor unions in France. And I think the movement is really resonating because it’s really hit a nerve here on a lot of issues that are important to French society. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Cole, I wanted to ask you — the French government has accused the left-wing political party France Unbowed of stoking the violence at the — or, some violence at these protests. Can you talk about the significance of this, especially as France is preparing for next year’s presidential elections? COLE STANGLER : Yeah. You know, I was talking about this earlier, and I think that this line that we’ve indeed heard from the government — I think it is both a great exaggeration of the mobilizing power of that party, La France Insoumise, led by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, and it’s also, I think, an insult to the collective intelligence of the high school students who are protesting. I mean, I don’t think it’s physically possible for a political party to have this broad of a reach. So, I think that’s sort of an easy excuse. But that’s — you know, that’s indicative of the approach the government has taken so far. And, you know, this question of police repression and police violence, which we heard about just earlier, has also been something that’s been kind of pushing the movement forward. A lot of French people, I think, have been shocked by the degree of the police violence. You know, we heard there was a 15-year-old who had his hand basically blown off by picking up a stun grenade that the police use here. We had another student who lost the use of his eye because he was hit by a rubber bullet. These are like, you know, low-grade, almost military kind of technologies that the police use in France. And it’s part of a policing strategy that has been in place for several years now. Many of your viewers might remember the yellow vest movement back in late 2018, where we had, you know, decentralized mass protests and a huge amount of violence, where you had protesters having — you know, losing their eyes, losing their hands. The difference here — and this is what makes it frightening — is we’re not talking about adults. We’re talking about literal high schoolers. We’re talking about 15-, 14-year-olds who are being beaten by police. And, you know, there have been incidents. We should just be clear: There have been incidents of, you know, people attacking police officers, at some points firefighters. But that is the extreme minority. And I think the much bigger story here, we’re talking about a democratic country where the police have been attacking high school students. And I think it’s — again, it’s documented. There’s been hundreds of complaints that have been filed with the French government to this effect. This French policing strategy that was used during the yellow vests is now being directed against high schoolers. And that’s also energizing this movement. A lot of people think it’s unacceptable. AMY GOODMAN : We’re going to go from Aix-en-Provence, where Cole Stangler is, to Lille, France, from the south to the north of France. Alys Rowlands is a university student and member of the national board of the French student union, also just at a protest. Alys, thanks so much for joining us. As we wrap up, what do you think it’s most important for us to understand about this mass protest that’s taking place in France, and what you’re demanding, and how this might even affect the national elections that are coming up next year in France? ALYS ROWLANDS : Yeah, absolutely. I think the most important thing here is that it started with the high schoolers. Today, it’s also university students, but we’ve seen also teachers. We’ve seen farmers. We’ve seen the yellow vesters who want to join again. We’ve seen everyone want to join this mobilization, because I think what’s very interesting about this one here is that everyone is deeply, deeply angry. We are completely fed up of the living conditions, the school conditions, the work conditions that we have, and everyone is really, really deeply angry. And that’s what’s really interesting at the moment. So, the students, like they’ve said, are being faced with really strong repression from the police forces. So, as they said before, there are many kids. This is children who are being shot at with rubber bullets and tear gas and water cannons, who are being chased, who are being, you know, arrested massively. And this is completely unheard of before. It’s only been a week of this mobilization with the different protests and schools being blocked, etc., and it’s already over 5,000 people arrested, and, as you said, mostly children. And so, this is completely different from things that we’ve seen before. And because France, it’s — quite often there are mobilizations and things, but this is completely a different proportion, because people are really deeply angry about what’s going on and the conditions that we are living in. And I think this will have an impact, because we’re already seeing things changing. But what people want right now, it’s not one reform. It’s not one thing. It’s a deep change in the system and more budgets for the public services in France, which is behind all of this. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Alys, what is your sense of the — excuse me — the response of adults, of the parents of these children, of the general society to the way that the government has reacted to the student protests? ALYS ROWLANDS : Yeah, that’s an interesting question, because we can see in protests loads of parents. And we’ve seen online, on TikTok and the different apps, that the teachers and parents have been joining the protests, because they understand that the students, the high schoolers especially, are really deeply angry and they are completely fed up of going to school and then there being rats and the ceiling falling down and chemical products in the ceiling that are giving us cancer. Like, it’s completely — it’s completely insane. And so, the parents and teachers, but also, much wider, the general population are completely with the mobilizations. But the media are only showing violence and this and that. But the true violence is the violence of the police, the violence of the repression. How is it possible that children, 14-year-olds, are having their eyes being blown off, their hands being blown off, their teeth being completely ripped out by these rubber bullets and tear gas? How is it possible that this is happening in France today? Five thousand people arrested, mostly children, how is this possible? The true violence is the violence of the state that we are being faced with all day, every day, all year. That’s the true violence: having no money, having difficulty finishing the month, having less and less help from the state, having to choose between eating and putting your heating on during the winter. It’s that kind of violence that we are faced with all year. And so, you know, the parents and the teachers and, wider, the general population are completely agreeing with the —everything that they want, the students, the high schoolers, the university students, but also much wider. Everyone has things they want to change. AMY GOODMAN : Alys Rowlands, we want to thank you for being with us from Lille, from the north of France, university student, member of the national board of the FSU , French student union. I also want to thank Cole Stangler, journalist based in France, covering politics and labor issues, joining us from Aix-en-Provence in the south, and Claire Vigneau, general secretary of the French student union, joining us from the streets of Rennes, where the massive protest also is taking place today, as it is across the country. And just to underscore something Juan said about the heat and the lack of air conditioning, this isn’t just a luxury. We’re talking about 8,000 people in France this summer died from heat. Coming up, we go to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where the death toll from Ebola has topped 4,000. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Freedom Is Free” by Chicano Batman.

articles.title: Ebola Death Toll in DRC Tops 4,000; Trump USAID Cuts Fuel Outbreak
articles.content: We go to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the site of the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history. Health authorities believe the outbreak first began in January but was not detected until May, in part due to cuts in global health investments, like the dismantling of USAID . Since then, over 8,000 cases have been recorded, with more than 4,000 fatalities so far. From Bunia, Ituri province, the epicenter of the outbreak, we speak to Congolese journalist Akilimali Chomachoma. Chomachoma describes the strain on the underfunded Congolese healthcare system as the disease spreads. Many frontline workers have not been paid for months. “We are seeing this outbreak emerge, and really unfurl, in a setting of decreased global health support,” says Craig Spencer, a doctor and public health expert based in the United States who contracted Ebola while on a medical mission to Guinea in 2014. “The U.S. has not shown up in the same way that it has in previous Ebola outbreaks.” Spencer also comments on the “unprecedented” measles outbreak in the United States, which he warns is likely to continue and lead to additional deaths.

articles.title: “Incredible Moment for the Borderlands”: Judge Blocks Border Wall Expansion in Big Bend & West Texas
articles.content: In a victory for environmentalists and immigration rights’ advocates, a federal judge in El Paso, Texas, has blocked further border wall construction inside Big Bend National Park. “We slammed the brakes on $7 billion worth of corrupt construction contracts,” says Laiken Jordahl, a national public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, which sued to block the expansion. “We have effectively stopped construction across West Texas, and it’s incredible.” Jordahl also responds to the Trump administration’s excavation of a 200-year-old cottonwood tree on the Arizona-Mexico border that had been protected by activists for months. “Watching those videos of them toppling this ancient tree that was very likely older than the border itself is symbolic of how DHS has treated the border region. They see our communities, our wildlife, our nature as a sacrifice zone,” says Jordahl.

articles.title: Brazilians Elect Eight Candidates from MST in 2026 Election
articles.content: 6.Oct.2026 - 11:22 São Paulo (SP) From the newsroom 16 candidaturas ligadas ao MST disputaram cargos nas Eleições 2026 | Crédito: Divulgação/MST Eight members of the Landless Rural Workers’ Movement, or MST, were elected to legislative bodies in the October 4 elections. This includes four lawmakers heading to Brazil’s lower house of Congress and four representatives to state legislatures. They were all elected, representing the Workers’ Party. They came from different states and regions of the country. Valmir Assunção, from Bahia; Rosa Amorim, from Pernambuco; Marcon, from Rio Grande do Sul; and João Daniel, from Sergipe, were all elected to Brazil’s Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of Congress. All four have a history of activism linked to the movement and standing up for agrarian reform. Rosa Amorim, who was already serving as a lawmaker in the Pernambuco Legislative Assembly, is the first female member of the MST to reach the Chamber of Deputies. She was born in the Normandia settlement in Caruaru. She began her activism with the MST during childhood and was elected to the Pernambuco Legislative Assembly in 2022. Valmir Assunção, João Daniel, and Marcon were re-elected. The MST also saw the re-election of Adão Pretto Filho, from Rio Grande do Sul; Marina do MST, from Rio de Janeiro; and Missias, from Ceará. In this election, MST member Camilo Daniel also won a seat in the Sergipe Legislative Assembly. Who was elected – Federal Deputies Valmir Assunção (PT-BA) Rosa Amorim (PT-PE) Marcon (PT-RS) João Daniel (PT-SE) State Legislative Assembly Adão Pretto Filho (PT-RS) Marina do MST (PT-RJ) Camilo Daniel (PT-SE) Missias (PT-CE)

articles.title: Israeli forces demolish Birzeit University’s martyrs memorial
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: At dawn on Monday, October 5, Israeli forces destroyed the martyrs’ memorial at Birzeit University. Basil Farraj, an assistant professor of philosophy and cultural studies at Birzeit University, told BreakThrough News that the Israeli forces came to the campus around a week ago to capture photos of the memorial, sparking suspicions that they may attempt to destroy it. Farraj suggests that the removal of the memorial came as part of Israel’s broader efforts to erase the Palestinian people’s collective memory and entrench cultural, social, and political hegemony over them, specifically at Birzeit University, due to its pioneering role in the Palestinian struggle against occupation. “The assault on the memorial constitutes a cowardly attempt that will never defeat the resilience of the Palestinian collective memory. It also reflects the failure of the Zionist project in the face of the Palestinian people’s struggle,” he emphasized. Meanwhile, the Right to Education Campaign issued a statement , condemning the offensive, and clarifying that it was carried out on the first day of the new academic year. “The destruction of a memorial to student martyrs is an assault on our collective memory, and our right to remember, preserve our history, and honour those who are part of Birzeit’s story,” the statement reads. “This attack comes within a broader pattern of scholasticide on Palestinian universities and the systematic disruption of academic life,” it continued. The campaign urged “universities, academics, students, human rights organizations, and governments worldwide to demand accountability, protect Palestinian educational institutions, and take concrete action to defend the right to education and academic freedom.” The university as a target In recent years, the Israeli forces have intensified their crackdown campaign on Palestinian universities across the occupied West Bank. There has been a particular focus on Birzeit University in northern Ramallah due to its pioneering role in the Palestinian prolonged struggle against the occupation. Not only have prominent scientists, political leaders, artists, and journalists graduate from the renowned Palestinian institution, but it has also long been called the “University of Martyrs” because dozens of its students and graduates have been killed at the hands of the Israeli military. Countless students have been arrested and the university campus has faced frequent military raids since 2002 . Read more: IOF abducts four Birzeit University female students at dawn

articles.title: The far right wins the first round in Brazil, but Lula isn’t done yet
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: On October 4, over 150 million Brazilians were called to the polls to elect their president, deputies, and governors, and to replace the majority of senators. The elections , for many, brought a major surprise. Although polls indicated a lead for the incumbent president, progressive Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva, far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro clinched first place. Flávio is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro who is currently serving a 27-year sentence for his involvement in an attempted coup against Lula in 2022. According to the final tally, Bolsonaro received 47.03% of the vote (56 million votes) while Lula received 45.16%, nearly 54 million votes. Thus, Bolsonaro’s lead amounts to just over 2 million votes. In third place is Augusto Cury, with 2.89%. He is followed by Renan Santos and Ronaldo Caiado, with 2.24% and 2.18%, respectively. The remaining candidates received less than 0.3%. A look at how the different regions of the country voted , a clear political divide between the north and the south of the country becomes apparent. The north (including states such as Amazonas, Pará, Amapá, Maranhão, Piauí, Bahia, Sergipe, Alagoas, Pernambuco, Paraíba, and Rio Grande do Norte) supported the continued presence of the state and the welfare policies proposed by Lula. For its part, including the northern state of Roraima, the south of the country clearly backed Bolsonaro’s neoliberal and pro-Trump agenda: Acre, Rondônia, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Goiás, Mato Grosso do Sul, Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo, Rio de Janeiro, Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul voted for Bolsonaro. On his X account, the far-right senator from the Liberal Party (PL) said : “Together, we’re going to build a new Brazil. A Brazil of prosperity! Tomorrow, you’ll stand before the ballot box and choose the future of our country, the future of our children, of this generation and the next. Change is in your hands. Brazil is going to win!” For his part, the president and candidate of the Workers’ Party (PT) said : “The result is often unexpected. You never get everything you want.” Yet, Lula, who has fought dozens of political battles, said: “[The runoff] is the time to show the true picture of Brazil today and of the Brazil we want.” To secure victory, Bolsonaro hopes to win over the votes of the candidates who finished behind the finalists – the majority of whom undoubtedly hold right-wing ideologies. Lula, however, can still turn the situation around if he manages to form the right alliances and win over voters who cast invalid ballots (about 3%), as well as those who abstained, who account for 21.08% of the total electorate. Senate, house of representatives, and governors And while Lula has expressed optimism about the possibility of turning the tide in the presidential runoff to be held on October 25, the political reality in Brazil has changed. Bolsonaro’s PL party has managed to double its number of senators: it won 19 of the 54 seats up for election out of a total of 81 senators. Among them, immediate family members of the former president, such as Michelle Bolsonaro and Carlos Bolsonaro, won seats. In total, the PL will hold more than a third of the Senate, while Lula’s PT will hold 9. This institution is particularly important because it approves or rejects the judges of the Federal Supreme Court (the country’s highest court) who are nominated by the president. This gives Bolsonaro significant ideological leverage, as he claims his father is being held in custody due to a conspiracy between political powers and a biased judicial system. In the elections for the Chamber of Deputies, which has 513 seats, the Bolsonaro camp also secured a significant victory. With 100% of the votes counted, the PL won 121 seats, while the Brazil of Hope Federation coalition (which includes Lula’s PT, the Green Party, and the Communist Party) won 88 seats. However, due to the method of seat allocation, Brazil favors a Chamber of Deputies with representation from many political forces. This is how the Progressive Union secured 87 seats, the Social Democratic Party 43, the Republicans 41, the Brazilian Democratic Movement 36, Podemos 27, the PSOL 15, as well as the Brazilian Socialist Party, among others. Thus, while the right has the numbers to secure a numerical advantage in the Chamber of Deputies, it will have to contend with deep-seated and historic internal contradictions that could complicate a potential Bolsonaro presidency. Similarly, if Lula manages to prevail in the runoff, he will face a highly complex Senate and Chamber of Deputies that could potentially oppose him. In the gubernatorial elections , the PL is also the biggest winner. Of 27 states, the Liberal Party has won six so far, while the PT, the Social Democratic Party, the PP, and the Republicans have each won three. Other states will have to elect their governors in a runoff election. The most talked-about result is the decisive victory in São Paulo by Tarcísio de Freitas, Jair Bolsonaro’s former Minister of Infrastructure, who defeated Fernando Haddad, Lula’s right-hand man. São Paulo is Brazil’s most populous state (46 million people) and home to the South American country’s most powerful economic hubs. A political future in doubt It has been repeatedly emphasized that, due to its economic and geopolitical importance, the elections in Brazil are of enormous significance for the future of Latin America. It is no coincidence that former US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger (who promoted a series of dictatorships in the region) said: “Whichever way Brazil leans, Latin America will lean that way.” The South American far right, which has enjoyed unprecedented electoral success in recent years, knows that without Brazil, its poker hand will always be incomplete. Uruguay indeed remains the only country in the region that does not share the views of Milei in Argentina, Kast in Chile, or De la Espriella in Colombia, but Brazil alone accounts for more than 50% of the region’s total GDP. Similarly, the left and the center know that a potential victory for Lula would be one of the last battles to be fought against the formidable advance of a right wing aligned with the foreign policies of Trump and Israel, with the most orthodox neoliberalism, and with the economic interests of capital magnates, including the big tech companies. And if Lula manages to recover from this defeat, it would mark a major shift in course for the legendary union leader – not only for Brazil but for the entire region. As Lula said, “now a different kind of campaign begins.” Both candidates will pull out all the stops to win control of South America’s most populous and powerful country. It certainly won’t be a “clean” campaign, but if one pays attention to the finalists’ statements, every means at their disposal will be used to achieve the coveted goal. US influence on the elections Political analysts have expressed concerns about alleged foreign interference in the elections. In July 2025, Trump had imposed 50% tariffs on Brazil over what he considered an unfair ruling against Jair Bolsonaro – whom the US president calls “his friend”. In August 2026, the United States revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington, a move denounced by Brasília as a violation of international law. Just last week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio ordered the closure of the US embassy in Brazil during the elections due to alleged “threats,” a move viewed by some political commentators as a tactic to create tension during the elections. During the first round of the presidential campaign, Trump did not make any direct statements of support for Flávio Bolsonaro. However, once the results were known, the US president told the press: “It’s a great victory – a close one, but a very, very great, incredible victory.” In this regard, it remains to be seen whether Trump will make some kind of direct statement in support of Bolsonaro’s candidacy – as he has done in past elections in Colombia, Argentina, Honduras, and elsewhere – in favor of far-right candidates who support his agenda. Or, even more importantly, whether he will make any kind of promise to the Brazilian people if Bolsonaro wins – or, worse yet, threaten them if they vote for Lula.

articles.title: Housing crisis leads to snap election in Spain
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced a snap election for late November after two housing bills were defeated in a parliamentary vote on Friday, October 2. The bills came amid widespread mass mobilizations demanding urgent action on the country’s housing crisis, following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets of approximately 50 cities over the weekend in support of these demands. “It is true that there are still many injustices to correct, many social goals to achieve, and many problems to solve – above all in the areas of inequality, public services, and access to housing,” Sánchez said in his speech on Monday, as he appealed to voters to give progressive forces more decisive electoral support to allow them to implement reforms more easily. Real estate speculation drives housing crisis While Sánchez’s administration has profiled itself as one of the more progressive governments in Europe in terms of international policy , national movements remain frustrated by the lack of decisiveness it has approached making changes at home – including in housing policy . For years, tenants unions have been warning against the different ways house-owners, particularly real estate speculation funds, have exacerbated housing insecurity for the general population. Existing anger spilled over as Maricarmen Abascal, an elderly tenant in Madrid, faced eviction from the home she had lived in for 70 years. After the development company Urbagestión Desarrollo e Inversión SL acquired the house Abascal lived in, they imposed a 275% rent increase that she was not able to meet, leading, after a lengthy legal process, to her eviction at the end of last month. Read more: Die Linke wins Berlin election with focus on socialization of housing The mobilizations that followed addressed a wider set of problems. “Maricarmen’s situation reflects a housing model that prioritizes real estate profits while abandoning the very people who built our neighborhoods over the decades,” Madrid Tenants’ Union (Sindicato de Inquilinas e Inquilinos de Madrid) warned. “Most serious of all is that this situation cannot be understood without considering the weight of laws inherited from the Franco regime that denied women basic rights,” the union emphasized in May. “The original contract was signed solely by Maricarmen’s father because the legal system of the time rendered women invisible within the family. Had that same contract been signed today, both parents would have been named as holders, and Maricarmen would remain fully protected.” “Yet an extremely restrictive interpretation of the regulations has ultimately weighed more heavily than social reality, than the desire to protect those who rent, and more than seventy years of roots in a neighborhood,” they added. “For the Madrid Tenants’ Union, the position is clear: no formalistic interpretation of the law can justify evicting an 87-year-old woman from the home where she has lived her entire life simply to boost the profitability of a real estate investment.” Unions promise building general strike for housing The protests formulated several demands to the government, including a ban on eviction of vulnerable tenants where alternative housing is not available; a limit to short-term and room rentals; a rent freeze; and an extension for contracts ending in 2026 and 2027. Such demands were generally by the public, as well as by trade unions. “Housing and work are not separate struggles,” unions wrote , pledging to work towards a general strike for housing. “The rise in rents is a direct transfer of wealth from the working class to rentierism. Our wages end up, month after month, in the pockets of the rentiers who control our homes.” The uproar pushed Sánchez’s government to reflect these demands in two bills it presented to parliament. Most considered this a significant breakthrough for the housing movement despite the official texts not fully corresponding to the protesters’ vocabulary and the vote taking place on two separate proposals. Watered down or not, right-wing and far-right parties voted against both bills. Read more: Far-right leaders gather in Madrid to “make Europe great again” “We have a democracy held hostage by rentiers and speculators,” the progressive party Podemos wrote as protests rolled out over the weekend. “The housing mobilization must keep growing and move toward a general strike until the speculators and those who defend them in the institutions have nowhere left to hide.” “Between now and November 29, the voices of all of us who want peace must be heard,” Irene Montero from Podemos added after the snap election announcement. “Those of us who want our sons and daughters to avoid war and to have healthcare and education, instead of money being spent on weapons; who want homes to live in; who want jobs and time to spend with our loved ones; and who want the cost of living to go down.”

articles.title: Iran welcomes the withdrawal of US forces from Iraq, calling it a victory for the resistance
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: The withdrawal of the remaining US troops from Iraq is a victory for the Iraqi nation and the resistance force in the region, Iran claimed on Thursday, October 1, also calling for greater cooperation between both the countries to achieve complete sovereignty for Iraq. “The US, despite possessing vast resources and equipment, has been expelled from Iraq, and the Iraqi people are celebrating this victory,” head of Iran’s Quds’ forces Esmail Qaani said during a program held in Tehran to mark the second anniversary of the Israeli assassination of Hezbollah leader Hasan Nasrallah. He thanked the “resistance of the Iraqi nation and the heroes of the Resistance Front” for making the end of the US occupation a reality. The US withdrew all its remaining forces from Iraq on September 30, as per the 2024 understanding between both the countries marking the conclusion of over a decade-long military presence in the country. The news of the withdrawal led to widespread celebrations in Baghdad and other parts of the country on Wednesday. The US occupied Iraq during the 2003 war which lasted until 2011 when it publicly stated that it withdrew all its forces. They were then re-deployed in 2014 as part of the international coalition fighting against the Islamic State or ISIS. Iraqi people, as well as the resistance groups in the country, have been demanding the withdrawal of all foreign troops from the country for years now. Their presence is seen as undermining the country’s sovereignty. Due to popular resistance, most of the foreign troops left the country by 2019 after a victory was declared over ISIS. Remaining US troops were redeployed to some bases in Baghdad and Erbil. In 2020, the Iraqi parliament adopted a resolution demanding the withdrawal of all remaining foreign troops from the country following popular protests over the US assassination of Qassem Solemani during a visit to Baghdad. Soleimani was the head of Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corp (IRGC) and key military strategist. Also an Iranian victory Qaani claimed that the US withdrawal from Iraq is also a victory for Iran which has been in support of the call on the ground that the presence of foreign troops in the region undermines regional security and stability. Qaani also linked the withdrawal to the setbacks the US faced in its war with Iran in the last seven months. Contrary to its expressed wish to force Iranians to surrender within days of the war launched on February 28, “they encountered a reality vastly different from their calculations,” he said. The US had used its military presence and the bases in Iraq to launch attacks across the border in Iran in the past and also during the ongoing war. This has prompted Iranian retaliations causing destruction and death of some of its servicemen. Iran has also accused that the US military’s presence in Iraq has been used by Israel for its clandestine operations inside the country. Reacting to US withdrawal from Iraq, IRGC said on Thursday that it is the beginning of its withdrawal from the entire region. Qaani expressed hope that in the aftermath of US troop withdrawal there will be increased coordination between the governments in Iraq and Iran for purging the remaining US influences on the country and creating a secure and sovereign Iraq. Though the US has withdrawn militarily, the legacy of its occupation still remains in Iraq. It continues to control Iraq’s economy by controlling the payments to its oil export s which are routed through the American Central Bank. Oil revenues made up 90% of the Iraqi government’s total budget and over 40% of its national GDP. Qaani accused that banning the Iranian airlines to Iraq and other countries in the region is a distraction used by the US to undermine the significance of its military defeat. Iraq and several other countries in the region complied with the US sanctions on Iranian airlines last month following Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s threats of secondary sanctions.
